passage:
Dear Joseph,

You asked why I did not come to Diwali dinner, so I will tell you plainly. Three months ago I stopped answering my father's calls. There were years of shouting and cutting remarks, and after my brother's wedding it got worse. The first week I felt lighter and slept through the night. In the second week I cried in the supermarket over a packet of his favourite biscuits. I keep asking myself whether I am punishing him. I do not think so. I think I am protecting myself. Still, I have written a note to myself: if he ever changes, and when I know I am safe, I will listen. For now I am keeping the door on the latch.

Love,
Anjali

qa.q: How long ago did Anjali stop answering the father's calls?
qa.a: Anjali stopped answering three months ago.

qa.q: What does Anjali's crying in the supermarket suggest?
qa.a: The relief is mixed with grief, and Anjali still misses something about the father.

qa.q: How can Anjali check that this comes from clarity and not anger?
qa.a: By asking whether the aim is protecting oneself rather than punishing, as Anjali does, and keeping the door ajar only where safety allows.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have asked about the missed dinner?
qa.a: Joseph noticed Anjali's absence and probably cares and is puzzled or worried.

grounding: The writer has cut contact with a father after long pain, feels relief mixed with grief, checks the motive and leaves the door only latched.

passage:
Wednesday.

It's been four months since I stopped answering Dad's calls. Manoj asked tonight if I miss him. I said no too quickly.

The truth is two things at once. I sleep better. I don't flinch when my phone rings. I don't spend Sundays bracing for his voice, the drunk voice that told me every week I was a useless son. Relief, every single day.

And then tonight a man at the bus stop had the same cough, and I had to walk away because my eyes were stinging. I'm grieving a dad I never really had.

I've been checking myself. Is this anger talking? I don't think so. I didn't cut him off after one bad fight. It was twenty years. My counsellor helped me decide it calmly, over months.

If he ever gets sober and gets help, maybe I'll open the door a crack. Only if it's safe.

I'm Thomas, and I'm allowed to have both feelings.

qa.q: How long has it been since Thomas stopped answering his father's calls?
What mixed feelings does Thomas have about the estrangement?
qa.a: Thomas feels daily relief, sleeping better and no longer flinching, and also grief for the dad he never really had.

qa.q: How does Thomas check that the choice is a wise one?
qa.a: Thomas asks whether anger is driving it, remembers it followed twenty years of pain and months of counselling, and keeps the door open only if it becomes safe.

qa.q: How does Manoj seem to see Thomas's situation?
qa.a: Manoj seems to care, gently asking whether Thomas misses his father.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young man who has cut contact with a parent after long pain, feeling relief mixed with grief, checking he acts from clarity and leaving the door open only if safe.

passage:
Mahima: Ammi called me again today. she asked about you
Farhan: what did you say
Mahima: that you're okay. are you?
Farhan: mostly. it's been a year since I stopped visiting. I don't miss the screaming
Farhan: I don't miss being told I ruined her life
Mahima: I know
Farhan: but on Eid I sat in my room and cried for an hour. I don't even know what for
Mahima: for the mum you wanted, maybe
Farhan: yeah. that
Mahima: do you ever think you did it out of anger?
Farhan: I asked myself that a lot. I think it was the only way to stay sane. the counsellor agreed
Farhan: if she ever gets help, really gets help, I'd meet her. somewhere public, with you there
Mahima: I'd come
Farhan: thank you for not pushing me
Mahima: you're my brother. I'm on your side

qa.q: How long has it been since Farhan stopped visiting?
What was Farhan feeling on Eid?
qa.a: Farhan felt deep grief, crying for an hour, perhaps for the mother he wished he had had.

qa.q: How has Farhan checked that the choice is wise?
qa.a: He asked himself whether anger drove it, talked it through with a counsellor, and keeps the door open only if his mother gets real help and it is safe.
Mahima listens without pushing, reflects his grief gently, and offers to be with him if he ever meets their mother.

grounding: A chat shows a young man who has cut contact with his mother after long pain, feeling relief mixed with grief, checking he acts from clarity and leaving the door open only if safe.
